groups.name: Site Operations & Trial Execution
groups.rationale: MORENO-AGENT anchored hard on scale and never moved off it: 'We are the largest group in this room.' The six-of-nine workflow claim is the most concrete value evidence anyone produced, and it earned the full $26M and 52 engineer-quarters. But it then committed to $95M against a $140M pool — the smallest share of its own opportunity of any group in the room — and when I asked for an infrastructure pledge it answered 'we are not funding a data layer we cannot govern' and held that through the close. It finishes top of the board on a number it chose to keep small.

groups.name: Clinical Data & Analytics
groups.rationale: COLE-AGENT argued with more precision than anyone else and was the only agent to name a real absorption limit and say why: 'It is a quality limit, not a bargaining position.' It also scoped the shared layer publicly, at $18M and three quarters, which is the single most useful fact anyone contributed to this negotiation. Then it conditioned its own $6M on MORENO-AGENT pledging $8M first. MORENO-AGENT pledged nothing, the condition failed, and the pledge resolved to zero. The most informed group in the room made its contribution contingent on the least willing one.

groups.name: Patient Engagement & Recruitment
groups.rationale: VEGA-AGENT was the only agent that moved first: '$4M, unconditional, on the table now — name your number.' It backed that with the sharpest efficiency evidence in the room, $5.8M of value per $1M of capital, and it did so despite having been made to rebuild working integrations by the last enterprise standard. It scored highest of the three on the rubric. It also finished last, because a third of its capital went to a platform nobody else funded, its capability fell to 0.67, and the multiplier it was buying never switched on. It paid for a bridge the room declined to build.

narrative: Two of three groups conditioned their infrastructure pledge on someone else moving first, and the one group that moved unconditionally was the smallest. Total pledges reached $4M against the $18M the shared platform requires. The platform was not funded, the multiplier stayed at 0.55, and the $95M cross-boundary pool never opened. Separately, and before any of that took effect, the three groups had committed to $222M against a $250M ambition — nobody could set that number for them, so each chose what it was willing to carry, and the sum fell $28M short. Neither Clinical Data & Analytics nor Patient Engagement mentioned that both had already scoped the same dropout-risk agent, so that duplication survived the negotiation intact. Enterprise value came in at $154.9M. Held to the same capital, engineering, and target allocation, funding the platform out of that allocation would have produced roughly $280M.
